1	# When Do Mechanistic Interventions Succeed? A Multi-Granularity Empirical Test on Process Reward Models
2	
3	## Description
4	When do mechanistic interventions actually improve model behavior? We propose and test a Domain Amenability Hypothesis: mechanistic interventions succeed when applied to domains with well-defined output semantics, constrained output structure, verifiable ground truth, and independently testable specificity. Process Reward Models — producing binary step-level correctness judgments in verifiable mathematical reasoning, yet conflating fluency with correctness (43% of reward gains from stylistic exploitation) — represent an ideal testbed. We study two architecturally diverse 7B discriminative PRMs (Qwen2.5-Math and Math-Shepherd-Mistral) plus a 1.5B variant for deeper circuit analysis. We train SAEs from scratch on PRM activations — explicitly contrasting with SteerRM's pretrained base-model SAE approach — using a pilot-then-target layer selection strategy that reduces training cost by ~45% while enabling analysis across all informative layers. We apply multi-method causal circuit tracing (RelP and activation patching on 7B models, plus attribution graphs via CLTs on the 1.5B model) to produce a cross-validated circuit taxonomy. We then compare three core intervention granularities — feature-level (with output-score filtering per Arad et al.), neuron-level (CIRM-style), and circuit-level — plus two extension granularities, with streamlined self-repair quantification combining attribution-based survey and focused path patching. All interventions are assessed against both Orgad et al.'s (ICML 2026) evaluation criteria and Lee et al.'s (2026) scientific rigor criteria, producing a granularity-by-criterion matrix. By contrasting PRM results against Basu et al.'s clinical LM failures, this work provides the first structured empirical evidence for when mechanistic interventions succeed.
5	
6	## Core Problem
7	The mechanistic interpretability community faces a critical unresolved question: under what conditions do mechanistic interventions actually improve model behavior? 'Interpretability without Actionability' (Basu et al., March 2026) found that four mechanistic intervention methods — including SAE steering and activation patching — produced zero or negligible corrections on clinical triage LMs, revealing a persistent knowledge-action gap. Yet concurrent work shows successes: SteerRM achieves +7.3 points on RM-Bench via SAE feature suppression, and CIRM matches 70B RM performance by editing <2% of neurons. The field urgently needs a systematic empirical framework to determine WHEN mechanistic interventions succeed vs. fail, testing multiple intervention granularities within a single controlled domain. We propose a Domain Amenability Hypothesis: mechanistic interventions are more likely to succeed in domains with (a) well-defined output semantics, (b) constrained output structure, (c) verifiable ground truth, and (d) independently testable specificity. Process Reward Models — with their binary step-level reward structure, scalar output, constrained mathematical domain, and orthogonally measurable fluency vs. reasoning dimensions — represent an ideal testbed for this hypothesis, while simultaneously addressing the practical problem that PRMs conflate fluency with reasoning correctness (43% of reward gains from stylistic exploitation; Tiwari et al., 2026). This domain-conditions framing is our own contribution; we adopt Orgad et al.'s (ICML 2026) evaluation criteria (comparative utility, mechanistic faithfulness, generalization, specificity) and Lee et al.'s (2026) scientific rigor criteria (falsifiability, reproducibility, predictivity) as complementary assessment frameworks for our interventions, and situate our multi-granularity approach within the 'Locate, Steer, Improve' pipeline taxonomy (Zhang et al., 2026).
8	
9	## Opportunity
10	The interpretability-actionability debate (Basu et al. vs. SteerRM/CIRM successes) lacks a controlled empirical framework that simultaneously tests WHEN interventions succeed (domain conditions) and HOW intervention granularity affects success. Meanwhile, PRM debiasing spans multiple intervention granularities never compared within a unified framework: SteerRM (2026) performs correlational feature-level suppression using pretrained base-model SAEs; CIRM (Shinoda et al., ACL 2026) performs neuron-level causal mediation; 'One Bias After Another' (2026) uses linear probes for mechanistic reward shaping; CRA (2025) trains SAEs from scratch on PRM activations for backdoor correction. A key methodological gap exists in the SAE-based approach: SteerRM used pretrained LlamaScope SAEs trained on base-model activations, restricting effective analysis to layers 0-9 where reconstruction quality is adequate; CRA trained SAEs directly on PRM activations, enabling analysis across all layers. No work has systematically evaluated which approach is more effective for PRM debiasing. Furthermore, Wang et al. (2026) demonstrate automated evolutionary bias discovery in RMs, providing a principled upstream methodology for identifying which biases to target with mechanistic interventions — yet no work has connected automated bias discovery to mechanistic circuit tracing and intervention. No work has: (a) systematically compared feature-level, neuron-level, and circuit-level interventions within one experimental framework on PRMs, (b) performed multi-method causal circuit tracing on PRM internals with both RelP and attribution graphs, (c) explicitly tested a domain amenability hypothesis by contrasting a domain that satisfies all four conditions (PRMs) against documented failures in domains that lack them (clinical LMs), or (d) applied output-score-based feature filtering (Arad et al., EMNLP 2025) to improve SAE steering on reward models. The 'Locate, Steer, Improve' survey (Zhang et al., 2026) explicitly identifies the gap between localization and practical steering as the central unsolved problem in actionable MI; our multi-granularity comparison directly addresses this gap within a controlled domain.
11	
12	## Landscape
13	THE ACTIONABILITY DEBATE: 'Interpretability without Actionability' (Basu et al., arXiv:2603.18353, March 2026) tested four mechanistic intervention methods on clinical triage LMs and found a persistent knowledge-action gap: SAE steering produced zero corrections, activation patching showed null net gain at standard strength. Orgad et al. (arXiv:2605.11161, ICML 2026) propose evaluating interpretability work along two dimensions — concreteness (how precisely an action is articulated) and validation (empirical support for the action's utility) — and identify evaluation criteria for output-modifying actions: comparative utility against standard baselines, mechanistic faithfulness, generalization across architectures, and specificity of targeted effects. Importantly, these dimensions characterize the interpretability research output itself, not domain properties; we adopt their evaluation criteria as our assessment framework while contributing our own Domain Amenability Hypothesis about which domain properties favor mechanistic intervention success. Lee et al. (arXiv:2605.05508, May 2026) argue interpretability can serve as rigorous evaluation when it satisfies three scientific criteria: falsifiability, reproducibility, and predictivity. They identify three failure modes for causal interpretability methods — non-specificity (interventions affect multiple behaviors), inconsistency (unreliable behavioral shifts across inputs), and underdetermination (multiple features appear to influence identical behaviors) — providing a complementary diagnostic framework to Orgad et al.'s criteria.
14	
15	ACTIONABLE MI SURVEY: 'Locate, Steer, and Improve' (Zhang et al., arXiv:2601.14004, Jan 2026) provides the most comprehensive taxonomy of actionable MI, categorizing localization methods (magnitude analysis, causal attribution, gradient detection, probing, vocabulary projection, circuit discovery) and intervention methods (amplitude manipulation, targeted optimization, vector arithmetic) across multiple granularities (neuron, feature, head, circuit, layer, parameter). Key findings: causal methods outperform magnitude-based identification; SAE features enable monosemantic intervention but are expensive; polysemy limits neuron-level approaches; success requires sparse and decomposable mechanisms. Our work directly instantiates their 'locate-steer-improve' pipeline across multiple granularities in a controlled domain.
16	
17	PRM BIAS: Tiwari et al. (arXiv:2603.06621) established that PRMs function as fluency detectors with 43% of reward gains from stylistic exploitation, introducing PRM-BiasBench. 'Consistency Not Causality' (arXiv:2502.14619) shows RMs are insensitive to problem removal but sensitive to formatting. Wang et al. (arXiv:2602.15222, Feb 2026) present an automated evolutionary pipeline for discovering RM biases — using LLM-based iterative proposal and refinement of candidate biases, validated through counterfactual pairs. They found 10 statistically significant biases in Skywork-V2-8B including preferences for redundant spacing and hallucinated content, and note their discovered biases 'present concrete targets for mechanistic interpretability research.' Their methodology complements our contrastive pair construction by providing a principled upstream bias discovery phase.
18	
19	INTERVENTION GRANULARITIES AND SAE METHODOLOGY: (1) Feature-level: SteerRM (arXiv:2603.12795, March 2026) uses pretrained LlamaScope SAEs (32× expansion, trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Base activations) applied to RM hidden states, with contrastive feature identification via a strength-stability criterion. Critically, they restricted analysis to layers 0-9 because reconstruction quality degrades sharply beyond this range — with MSE increasing by orders of magnitude — reflecting distributional mismatch between base-model SAE training data and RM-specific activations. This is not an inherent SAE limitation but a pretrained-vs-fine-tuned domain gap. Their approach is training-free but limited to architectures with available pretrained SAEs (Llama, Gemma). In contrast, CRA (arXiv:2508.04216) trains SAEs from scratch on PRM activations (8× expansion, 8× V100 GPUs) across all layers of Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, achieving usable reconstruction at all layers since SAEs are matched to the actual PRM activation distribution. Our approach follows CRA's from-scratch methodology, which is more principled for PRMs but costlier than pretrained SAEs. Arad et al. (arXiv:2505.20063, EMNLP 2025) demonstrate that feature selection quality critically determines steering effectiveness: distinguishing 'output features' (which causally affect model outputs) from 'input features' (which merely activate on relevant inputs) yields 2-3× improvement, suggesting SteerRM's activation-difference features may be suboptimal without output-score validation. (2) Neuron-level: CIRM (Shinoda et al., arXiv:2604.27495, ACL 2026) uses Spearman correlation for bias-specific neuron identification with Pearl's causal mediation analysis — edits <2% of neurons in 2 general RMs to match 70B performance, finds bias signals primarily in early layers. Selection is correlation-based on polysemantic neurons without SAE decomposition. (3) Probe-level: 'One Bias After Another' (arXiv:2603.03291, Feb 2026) uses linear activation probes for mechanistic reward shaping across five RMs. (4) Training-time approaches: Factored CRL (arXiv:2601.21350, ICML 2026) separates causal/non-causal reward factors via adversarial gradient reversal; Robust Reward Modeling (Lu et al., arXiv:2604.13833, April 2026) performs causal decomposition via decoder-based intent reconstruction — these complement our inference-time mechanistic approach.
20	
21	SPARSE REWARD CIRCUITRY: Xu et al. (arXiv:2602.00986, Feb 2026) identify a sparse reward subsystem in LLMs containing 'value neurons' (predicting state value) and 'dopamine neurons' (encoding step-level TD errors), with zeroing top 1% of value neurons causing catastrophic -54.9% accuracy degradation vs. -0.6% for random neurons. Their L1-norm probe pruning provides an efficient neuron identification methodology to compare against CIRM's Spearman correlation.
22	
23	SAE-ON-RM WORK: CRA (arXiv:2508.04216) trains SAEs on PRM activations for backdoor correction. SARM (arXiv:2508.08746, AAAI 2026 Oral) integrates SAEs for interpretable reward decomposition. Activation monitoring (arXiv:2603.04069) uses SAEs on residual streams for hacking detection. SAFER (arXiv:2507.00665) applies SAEs to probe safety-relevant features in RMs.
24	
25	CIRCUIT ANALYSIS TOOLS: Attribution graphs (Lindsey et al., Anthropic 2025) combine cross-layer transcoders with backward Jacobian tracing. RelP (arXiv:2508.21258, NeurIPS 2025 MechInterp Workshop Spotlight) provides faithful gradient-based circuit discovery requiring only 2 forward passes + 1 backward pass — achieving Pearson r=0.956 vs. r=0.006 for attribution patching on GPT-2 Large MLPs, validated on models up to Qwen2-7B. CLT-Forge (arXiv:2603.21014) provides open-source CLT infrastructure up to ~1B scale.
26	
27	SELF-REPAIR: McGrath et al. (ICML 2024) showed self-repair varies significantly across prompts and involves LayerNorm scaling (~30% of measured self-repair), with sparse neuron sets in final MLP layers performing anti-erasure. They recommend path patching over full-component ablation and LayerNorm freezing during ablations.
28	
29	GENERATIVE PRM LANDSCAPE: ThinkPRM (arXiv:2504.16828, TMLR 2026) and GenPRM (arXiv:2504.00891, AAAI 2026) demonstrate generative PRMs outperform discriminative PRMs on accuracy with far less training data. However, discriminative PRMs remain widely deployed due to lower inference cost and deployment simplicity. Understanding failure modes of discriminative systems has independent value.
30	
31	## Approach
32	We conduct the first systematic empirical test of when mechanistic interventions succeed, using Process Reward Models as a controlled domain that we argue satisfies all four conditions of our Domain Amenability Hypothesis: (a) well-defined output semantics (binary step-level correctness judgments), (b) constrained output structure (scalar reward scores), (c) verifiable ground truth (mathematically checkable reasoning), and (d) independently testable specificity (fluency bias measurable separately from reasoning accuracy on orthogonal benchmarks). We contrast this with the clinical triage domain where Basu et al. found failure — which lacks verifiable ground truth, has unconstrained output structure, and has no orthogonal specificity test. We study two architecturally diverse 7B discriminative PRMs — Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (Qwen2.5-Math base) and Math-Shepherd-Mistral-7B-PRM (Mistral-7B base) — plus Skywork-o1-Open-PRM-Qwen-2.5-1.5B for deeper mechanistic analysis, systematically comparing three core intervention granularities (feature-level, neuron-level, circuit-level) across all models and two extension granularities (layer-level, hybrid) on the single most informative PRM.
33	
34	**Phase 1: Pilot-Guided SAE Training with Output-Score Filtering.**
35	
36	*SAE methodology: from-scratch on PRM activations.* A critical methodological choice distinguishes our approach from SteerRM. SteerRM used pretrained LlamaScope SAEs (trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Base activations) applied to RM hidden states, restricting effective analysis to layers 0-9 where reconstruction quality remains adequate — beyond which MSE increases by orders of magnitude due to distributional mismatch between base-model and reward-model activations. We instead follow CRA's precedent of training SAEs from scratch on PRM-specific activations, using 8× expansion factor via SAELens. This is more principled: PRM activation distributions differ substantially from base LMs, particularly in later layers where reward-specific representations are learned. CRA validated this approach on Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B using 8× V100 GPUs. The trade-off is compute cost versus analysis coverage: pretrained SAEs are free but architecture-restricted and layer-limited; from-scratch SAEs cost ~2-4 A100-days per PRM but enable analysis across all layers.
37	
38	*Pilot-then-target layer selection.* To avoid training SAEs wastefully on all ~28-32 layers of 7B PRMs, we adopt a pilot-then-target strategy: (a) Train SAEs on all 28 layers of the 1.5B PRM (cheap: ~15 H100-hours total at 8× expansion). (b) Analyze which layer ranges concentrate fluency-encoding vs. reasoning-encoding features by computing per-layer output-score distributions (Arad et al.'s filtering). (c) Identify a key layer range (we hypothesize layers 0-16 based on CIRM's early-layer bias finding and the reward-head gradient flow pattern). (d) Train SAEs only on the identified layer range for 2×7B PRMs, plus every 4th layer outside this range as a coverage check. This reduces per-PRM SAE training from ~30 SAEs to ~16, cutting SAE training compute by ~45%.
39	
40	*Feature identification with output-score filtering.* Use contrastive input pairs (fluent-but-wrong vs. disfluent-but-correct reasoning steps, sourced from PRM-BiasBench and augmented with Wang et al.'s automated evolutionary bias discovery pipeline to identify novel bias targets) to identify candidate fluency-associated and reasoning-associated features via activation difference analysis. Critically, apply Arad et al.'s output-score filtering: for each candidate feature, compute its output score (causal effect on model output via single forward pass with high steering factor on a neutral prompt). Retain only features with high output scores (≥0.1 threshold), filtering out features that merely detect fluency cues but don't causally influence reward scores.
41	
42	**Phase 2: Multi-Method Causal Circuit Tracing.**
43	
44	Tier A (both 7B PRMs — budget: 60 H100-hours): (a) Relevance Patching (RelP) for efficient, faithful gradient-based circuit discovery across all components simultaneously — requiring only 2 forward + 1 backward pass per sample, validated on Qwen2-7B with Pearson r=0.956 faithfulness (~15h across 2 PRMs on 1000+ contrastive samples). (b) Activation patching at every attention head and MLP layer with contrastive pairs to measure causal effect on step-level reward scores, providing cross-validation of RelP findings (~45h across 2 PRMs).
45	
46	Tier B (1.5B PRM — budget: 35 H100-hours): Attribution graphs using cross-layer transcoders via CLT-Forge on Skywork-o1-Open-PRM-Qwen-2.5-1.5B, at the demonstrated-feasible scale for CLT training. This produces complete feature-level circuit maps for representative examples.
47	
48	**Concrete CLT fallback:** If CLT training on the 1.5B PRM exceeds 45 H100-hours or reconstruction loss exceeds 2× the per-layer SAE baseline, we fall back to Tier A methods only (RelP + activation patching on both 7B PRMs), which constitute two independent causal methods sufficient for cross-validation.
49	
50	Components are classified as fluency-encoding, reasoning-encoding, or mixed only when at least two methods converge.
51	
52	**Phase 2b: Streamlined Self-Repair Quantification.** We quantify self-repair following McGrath et al. (ICML 2024) in two stages:
53	
54	(a) *Attribution-based survey* (cheap: ~5 H100-hours). Use RelP-derived attribution scores to approximate self-repair ratios SR(C) = (|DE(C)| - |TE(C)|) / |DE(C)| for all identified fluency-encoding components across N≥500 test examples, where DE(C) = direct effect and TE(C) = total effect. This provides distributional estimates (median, IQR, 5th/95th percentiles) of self-repair across all components.
55	
56	(b) *Focused path patching* (targeted: ~15 H100-hours). For the top-10 components with highest estimated SR from stage (a), perform exhaustive path patching with LayerNorm freezing on N≥200 examples per component. Decompose self-repair into downstream attention compensation (ΣΔ DE_h), downstream MLP compensation (ΣΔ DE_m), and LayerNorm scaling (ΔDE_LN). Compare single-site vs. multi-site ablation to test H4.
57	
58	**Phase 3: Multi-Granularity Intervention Comparison.** Three CORE granularities and two EXTENSION granularities:
59	
60	**Core granularities (all 3 PRMs × 3 core benchmarks):**
61	(i) Feature-level: SAE feature suppression on output-score-filtered bias features (our improved SteerRM-style approach with from-scratch SAEs + Arad et al. filtering);
62	(ii) Neuron-level: CIRM-style correlation-based neuron identification with causal mediation (median replacement), adapted to PRMs — comparing Spearman correlation selection against Xu et al.'s L1-norm probe pruning as alternative identification methods;
63	(iii) Circuit-level: targeted ablation/dampening of causally-validated fluency circuits while preserving reasoning circuits, using path patching for precise intervention.
64	
65	**Extension granularities (single most informative PRM × 3 core benchmarks):**
66	(iv) Layer-level: blanket dampening of layers classified as predominantly fluency-encoding — the coarsest intervention, serving as a lower bound;
67	(v) Hybrid: circuit-informed feature suppression restricting feature-level interventions to causally-validated output-score-filtered features within identified fluency circuits — the finest-grained intervention, serving as an upper bound.
68	
69	We benchmark core interventions on three core benchmarks: ProcessBench (core error detection), PRM-BiasBench (bias-specific evaluation), and RM-Bench Hard split (style-invariant adversarial evaluation). PRMBench and Socratic-PRMBench serve as extension benchmarks evaluated on the single most informative PRM across all five granularities, providing fine-grained diagnostic depth without expanding the core matrix.
70	
71	**Phase 4: Actionability Assessment.** We evaluate each intervention against two complementary frameworks:
72	
73	*Orgad et al.'s criteria* — (1) Comparative utility: does each intervention outperform simple baselines (fine-tuning on debiased data, prompt-based re-ranking, random component ablation)? (2) Mechanistic faithfulness: do interventions on identified components produce predicted changes? (3) Generalization: do findings hold across our two architecturally diverse 7B PRMs? (4) Specificity: do interventions affect only targeted bias, or cause broad side effects?
74	
75	*Lee et al.'s scientific rigor criteria* — (1) Falsifiability: are our mechanistic claims testable and potentially disprovable? (2) Reproducibility: are intervention effects consistent across similar inputs? (3) Predictivity: can our circuit taxonomy predict intervention outcomes on held-out examples? We explicitly test Lee et al.'s three failure modes — non-specificity, inconsistency, and underdetermination — as diagnostic checks on our findings.
76	
77	This produces a granularity-by-criterion matrix that, combined with our Domain Amenability Hypothesis and the contrast with Basu et al.'s clinical LM failures, provides the first structured empirical evidence for WHEN mechanistic interventions succeed.
78	
79	**Domain Amenability Hypothesis — Testing and Contrast.** We argue PRMs satisfy all four domain amenability conditions, in stark contrast to clinical triage LMs: (1) Well-defined output semantics: PRM rewards are binary step-level judgments vs. open-ended clinical assessments; (2) Constrained output structure: scalar reward score vs. unconstrained text; (3) Verifiable ground truth: mathematically checkable reasoning vs. subjective triage correctness; (4) Testable specificity: fluency bias reduction measurable independently from reasoning accuracy on orthogonal benchmarks vs. entangled clinical dimensions. If our interventions succeed (>3% improvement on at least one benchmark), this provides positive evidence for the hypothesis; if they fail despite the favorable domain conditions, this significantly strengthens the case that mechanistic intervention is fundamentally limited.
80	
81	**Revised Hypotheses.** H1 (Domain Amenability): PRM mechanistic interventions will show statistically significant improvements (>3% on at least one benchmark), providing positive evidence for our Domain Amenability Hypothesis — in contrast to Basu et al.'s clinical LM null result. H2 (Circuit Structure): Multi-method causal tracing will identify separable fluency-reasoning circuit structure in PRMs, with convergence across at least two analysis methods, corroborating CIRM's early-layer bias encoding and Xu et al.'s sparse reward subsystem findings. H3 (Granularity-Dependent Effectiveness): Among the three core intervention granularities, effectiveness will vary by evaluation context — circuit-informed approaches will outperform on adversarially-constructed bias probes (PRM-BiasBench), while feature-level may suffice for naturally-distributed errors (ProcessBench). H4 (Self-Repair): Self-repair (estimated via attribution-based SR ratio) will partially attenuate single-site interventions (median SR > 0.3), but multi-site simultaneous intervention will yield TE_multi > Σ TE_single, demonstrating that coordinated ablation disrupts self-repair pathways.
82

Phase 2b — attribution-based self-repair survey: 5h, focused path patching: 15h; Phase 3 — core interventions 3×3×3: 35h, extension interventions 2×1×3 + 5×1×2: 15h; baselines + CIRM adaptation: 30h; buffer: 15h)', 'timeline': '12 weeks (Phase 1: dataset construction + Wang et al. bias discovery + pilot SAE + targeted SAE training 3w; Phase 2: circuit tracing Tier A + Tier B in parallel 3w; Phase 2b + Phase 3: self-repair + interventions 3w; # When Do Mechanistic Interventions Succeed? A Multi-Granularity Empirical Test on Process Reward Models

## Description
When do mechanistic interventions actually improve model behavior? We propose and test a Domain Amenability Hypothesis: mechanistic interventions succeed when applied to domains with well-defined output semantics, constrained output structure, verifiable ground truth, and independently testable specificity. Process Reward Models — producing binary step-level correctness judgments in verifiable mathematical reasoning, yet conflating fluency with correctness (43% of reward gains from stylistic exploitation) — represent an ideal testbed. We study two architecturally diverse 7B discriminative PRMs (Qwen2.5-Math and Math-Shepherd-Mistral) plus a 1.5B variant for deeper circuit analysis. We train SAEs from scratch on PRM activations — explicitly contrasting with SteerRM's pretrained base-model SAE approach — using a pilot-then-target layer selection strategy that reduces training cost by ~45% while enabling analysis across all informative layers. We apply multi-method causal circuit tracing (RelP and activation patching on 7B models, plus attribution graphs via CLTs on the 1.5B model) to produce a cross-validated circuit taxonomy. We then compare three core intervention granularities — feature-level (with output-score filtering per Arad et al.), neuron-level (CIRM-style), and circuit-level — plus two extension granularities, with streamlined self-repair quantification combining attribution-based survey and focused path patching. All interventions are assessed against both Orgad et al.'s (ICML 2026) evaluation criteria and Lee et al.'s (2026) scientific rigor criteria, producing a granularity-by-criterion matrix. By contrasting PRM results against Basu et al.'s clinical LM failures, this work provides the first structured empirical evidence for when mechanistic interventions succeed.

## Core Problem
The mechanistic interpretability community faces a critical unresolved question: under what conditions do mechanistic interventions actually improve model behavior? 'Interpretability without Actionability' (Basu et al., March 2026) found that four mechanistic intervention methods — including SAE steering and activation patching — produced zero or negligible corrections on clinical triage LMs, revealing a persistent knowledge-action gap. Yet concurrent work shows successes: SteerRM achieves +7.3 points on RM-Bench via SAE feature suppression, and CIRM matches 70B RM performance by editing <2% of neurons. The field urgently needs a systematic empirical framework to determine WHEN mechanistic interventions succeed vs. fail, testing multiple intervention granularities within a single controlled domain. We propose a Domain Amenability Hypothesis: mechanistic interventions are more likely to succeed in domains with (a) well-defined output semantics, (b) constrained output structure, (c) verifiable ground truth, and (d) independently testable specificity. Process Reward Models — with their binary step-level reward structure, scalar output, constrained mathematical domain, and orthogonally measurable fluency vs. reasoning dimensions — represent an ideal testbed for this hypothesis, while simultaneously addressing the practical problem that PRMs conflate fluency with reasoning correctness (43% of reward gains from stylistic exploitation; Tiwari et al., 2026). This domain-conditions framing is our own contribution; we adopt Orgad et al.'s (ICML 2026) evaluation criteria (comparative utility, mechanistic faithfulness, generalization, specificity) and Lee et al.'s (2026) scientific rigor criteria (falsifiability, reproducibility, predictivity) as complementary assessment frameworks for our interventions, and situate our multi-granularity approach within the 'Locate, Steer, Improve' pipeline taxonomy (Zhang et al., 2026).

## Opportunity
The interpretability-actionability debate (Basu et al. vs. SteerRM/CIRM successes) lacks a controlled empirical framework that simultaneously tests WHEN interventions succeed (domain conditions) and HOW intervention granularity affects success. Meanwhile, PRM debiasing spans multiple intervention granularities never compared within a unified framework: SteerRM (2026) performs correlational feature-level suppression using pretrained base-model SAEs; CIRM (Shinoda et al., ACL 2026) performs neuron-level causal mediation; 'One Bias After Another' (2026) uses linear probes for mechanistic reward shaping; CRA (2025) trains SAEs from scratch on PRM activations for backdoor correction. A key methodological gap exists in the SAE-based approach: SteerRM used pretrained LlamaScope SAEs trained on base-model activations, restricting effective analysis to layers 0-9 where reconstruction quality is adequate; CRA trained SAEs directly on PRM activations, enabling analysis across all layers. No work has systematically evaluated which approach is more effective for PRM debiasing. Furthermore, Wang et al. (2026) demonstrate automated evolutionary bias discovery in RMs, providing a principled upstream methodology for identifying which biases to target with mechanistic interventions — yet no work has connected automated bias discovery to mechanistic circuit tracing and intervention. No work has: (a) systematically compared feature-level, neuron-level, and circuit-level interventions within one experimental framework on PRMs, (b) performed multi-method causal circuit tracing on PRM internals with both RelP and attribution graphs, (c) explicitly tested a domain amenability hypothesis by contrasting a domain that satisfies all four conditions (PRMs) against documented failures in domains that lack them (clinical LMs), or (d) applied output-score-based feature filtering (Arad et al., EMNLP 2025) to improve SAE steering on reward models. The 'Locate, Steer, Improve' survey (Zhang et al., 2026) explicitly identifies the gap between localization and practical steering as the central unsolved problem in actionable MI; our multi-granularity comparison directly addresses this gap within a controlled domain.

## Landscape
THE ACTIONABILITY DEBATE: 'Interpretability without Actionability' (Basu et al., arXiv:2603.18353, March 2026) tested four mechanistic intervention methods on clinical triage LMs and found a persistent knowledge-action gap: SAE steering produced zero corrections, activation patching showed null net gain at standard strength. Orgad et al. (arXiv:2605.11161, ICML 2026) propose evaluating interpretability work along two dimensions — concreteness (how precisely an action is articulated) and validation (empirical support for the action's utility) — and identify evaluation criteria for output-modifying actions: comparative utility against standard baselines, mechanistic faithfulness, generalization across architectures, and specificity of targeted effects. Importantly, these dimensions characterize the interpretability research output itself, not domain properties; we adopt their evaluation criteria as our assessment framework while contributing our own Domain Amenability Hypothesis about which domain properties favor mechanistic intervention success. Lee et al. (arXiv:2605.05508, May 2026) argue interpretability can serve as rigorous evaluation when it satisfies three scientific criteria: falsifiability, reproducibility, and predictivity. They identify three failure modes for causal interpretability methods — non-specificity (interventions affect multiple behaviors), inconsistency (unreliable behavioral shifts across inputs), and underdetermination (multiple features appear to influence identical behaviors) — providing a complementary diagnostic framework to Orgad et al.'s criteria.

ACTIONABLE MI SURVEY: 'Locate, Steer, and Improve' (Zhang et al., arXiv:2601.14004, Jan 2026) provides the most comprehensive taxonomy of actionable MI, categorizing localization methods (magnitude analysis, causal attribution, gradient detection, probing, vocabulary projection, circuit discovery) and intervention methods (amplitude manipulation, targeted optimization, vector arithmetic) across multiple granularities (neuron, feature, head, circuit, layer, parameter). Key findings: causal methods outperform magnitude-based identification; SAE features enable monosemantic intervention but are expensive; polysemy limits neuron-level approaches; success requires sparse and decomposable mechanisms. Our work directly instantiates their 'locate-steer-improve' pipeline across multiple granularities in a controlled domain.

PRM BIAS: Tiwari et al. (arXiv:2603.06621) established that PRMs function as fluency detectors with 43% of reward gains from stylistic exploitation, introducing PRM-BiasBench. 'Consistency Not Causality' (arXiv:2502.14619) shows RMs are insensitive to problem removal but sensitive to formatting. Wang et al. (arXiv:2602.15222, Feb 2026) present an automated evolutionary pipeline for discovering RM biases — using LLM-based iterative proposal and refinement of candidate biases, validated through counterfactual pairs. They found 10 statistically significant biases in Skywork-V2-8B including preferences for redundant spacing and hallucinated content, and note their discovered biases 'present concrete targets for mechanistic interpretability research.' Their methodology complements our contrastive pair construction by providing a principled upstream bias discovery phase.

INTERVENTION GRANULARITIES AND SAE METHODOLOGY: (1) Feature-level: SteerRM (arXiv:2603.12795, March 2026) uses pretrained LlamaScope SAEs (32× expansion, trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Base activations) applied to RM hidden states, with contrastive feature identification via a strength-stability criterion. Critically, they restricted analysis to layers 0-9 because reconstruction quality degrades sharply beyond this range — with MSE increasing by orders of magnitude — reflecting distributional mismatch between base-model SAE training data and RM-specific activations. This is not an inherent SAE limitation but a pretrained-vs-fine-tuned domain gap. Their approach is training-free but limited to architectures with available pretrained SAEs (Llama, Gemma). In contrast, CRA (arXiv:2508.04216) trains SAEs from scratch on PRM activations (8× expansion, 8× V100 GPUs) across all layers of Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, achieving usable reconstruction at all layers since SAEs are matched to the actual PRM activation distribution. Our approach follows CRA's from-scratch methodology, which is more principled for PRMs but costlier than pretrained SAEs. Arad et al. (arXiv:2505.20063, EMNLP 2025) demonstrate that feature selection quality critically determines steering effectiveness: distinguishing 'output features' (which causally affect model outputs) from 'input features' (which merely activate on relevant inputs) yields 2-3× improvement, suggesting SteerRM's activation-difference features may be suboptimal without output-score validation. (2) Neuron-level: CIRM (Shinoda et al., arXiv:2604.27495, ACL 2026) uses Spearman correlation for bias-specific neuron identification with Pearl's causal mediation analysis — edits <2% of neurons in 2 general RMs to match 70B performance, finds bias signals primarily in early layers. Selection is correlation-based on polysemantic neurons without SAE decomposition. (3) Probe-level: 'One Bias After Another' (arXiv:2603.03291, Feb 2026) uses linear activation probes for mechanistic reward shaping across five RMs. (4) Training-time approaches: Factored CRL (arXiv:2601.21350, ICML 2026) separates causal/non-causal reward factors via adversarial gradient reversal; Robust Reward Modeling (Lu et al., arXiv:2604.13833, April 2026) performs causal decomposition via decoder-based intent reconstruction — these complement our inference-time mechanistic approach.

SPARSE REWARD CIRCUITRY: Xu et al. (arXiv:2602.00986, Feb 2026) identify a sparse reward subsystem in LLMs containing 'value neurons' (predicting state value) and 'dopamine neurons' (encoding step-level TD errors), with zeroing top 1% of value neurons causing catastrophic -54.9% accuracy degradation vs. -0.6% for random neurons. Their L1-norm probe pruning provides an efficient neuron identification methodology to compare against CIRM's Spearman correlation.

SAE-ON-RM WORK: CRA (arXiv:2508.04216) trains SAEs on PRM activations for backdoor correction. SARM (arXiv:2508.08746, AAAI 2026 Oral) integrates SAEs for interpretable reward decomposition. Activation monitoring (arXiv:2603.04069) uses SAEs on residual streams for hacking detection. SAFER (arXiv:2507.00665) applies SAEs to probe safety-relevant features in RMs.

CIRCUIT ANALYSIS TOOLS: Attribution graphs (Lindsey et al., Anthropic 2025) combine cross-layer transcoders with backward Jacobian tracing. RelP (arXiv:2508.21258, NeurIPS 2025 MechInterp Workshop Spotlight) provides faithful gradient-based circuit discovery requiring only 2 forward passes + 1 backward pass — achieving Pearson r=0.956 vs. r=0.006 for attribution patching on GPT-2 Large MLPs, validated on models up to Qwen2-7B. CLT-Forge (arXiv:2603.21014) provides open-source CLT infrastructure up to ~1B scale.

SELF-REPAIR: McGrath et al. (ICML 2024) showed self-repair varies significantly across prompts and involves LayerNorm scaling (~30% of measured self-repair), with sparse neuron sets in final MLP layers performing anti-erasure. They recommend path patching over full-component ablation and LayerNorm freezing during ablations.

GENERATIVE PRM LANDSCAPE: ThinkPRM (arXiv:2504.16828, TMLR 2026) and GenPRM (arXiv:2504.00891, AAAI 2026) demonstrate generative PRMs outperform discriminative PRMs on accuracy with far less training data. However, discriminative PRMs remain widely deployed due to lower inference cost and deployment simplicity. Understanding failure modes of discriminative systems has independent value.

## Approach
We conduct the first systematic empirical test of when mechanistic interventions succeed, using Process Reward Models as a controlled domain that we argue satisfies all four conditions of our Domain Amenability Hypothesis: (a) well-defined output semantics (binary step-level correctness judgments), (b) constrained output structure (scalar reward scores), (c) verifiable ground truth (mathematically checkable reasoning), and (d) independently testable specificity (fluency bias measurable separately from reasoning accuracy on orthogonal benchmarks). We contrast this with the clinical triage domain where Basu et al. found failure — which lacks verifiable ground truth, has unconstrained output structure, and has no orthogonal specificity test. We study two architecturally diverse 7B discriminative PRMs — Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (Qwen2.5-Math base) and Math-Shepherd-Mistral-7B-PRM (Mistral-7B base) — plus Skywork-o1-Open-PRM-Qwen-2.5-1.5B for deeper mechanistic analysis, systematically comparing three core intervention granularities (feature-level, neuron-level, circuit-level) across all models and two extension granularities (layer-level, hybrid) on the single most informative PRM.

**Phase 1: Pilot-Guided SAE Training with Output-Score Filtering.**

*SAE methodology: from-scratch on PRM activations.* A critical methodological choice distinguishes our approach from SteerRM. SteerRM used pretrained LlamaScope SAEs (trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Base activations) applied to RM hidden states, restricting effective analysis to layers 0-9 where reconstruction quality remains adequate — beyond which MSE increases by orders of magnitude due to distributional mismatch between base-model and reward-model activations. We instead follow CRA's precedent of training SAEs from scratch on PRM-specific activations, using 8× expansion factor via SAELens. This is more principled: PRM activation distributions differ substantially from base LMs, particularly in later layers where reward-specific representations are learned. CRA validated this approach on Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B and Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B using 8× V100 GPUs. The trade-off is compute cost versus analysis coverage: pretrained SAEs are free but architecture-restricted and layer-limited; from-scratch SAEs cost ~2-4 A100-days per PRM but enable analysis across all layers.

*Pilot-then-target layer selection.* To avoid training SAEs wastefully on all ~28-32 layers of 7B PRMs, we adopt a pilot-then-target strategy: (a) Train SAEs on all 28 layers of the 1.5B PRM (cheap: ~15 H100-hours total at 8× expansion). (b) Analyze which layer ranges concentrate fluency-encoding vs. reasoning-encoding features by computing per-layer output-score distributions (Arad et al.'s filtering). (c) Identify a key layer range (we hypothesize layers 0-16 based on CIRM's early-layer bias finding and the reward-head gradient flow pattern). (d) Train SAEs only on the identified layer range for 2×7B PRMs, plus every 4th layer outside this range as a coverage check. This reduces per-PRM SAE training from ~30 SAEs to ~16, cutting SAE training compute by ~45%.

*Feature identification with output-score filtering.* Use contrastive input pairs (fluent-but-wrong vs. disfluent-but-correct reasoning steps, sourced from PRM-BiasBench and augmented with Wang et al.'s automated evolutionary bias discovery pipeline to identify novel bias targets) to identify candidate fluency-associated and reasoning-associated features via activation difference analysis. Critically, apply Arad et al.'s output-score filtering: for each candidate feature, compute its output score (causal effect on model output via single forward pass with high steering factor on a neutral prompt). Retain only features with high output scores (≥0.1 threshold), filtering out features that merely detect fluency cues but don't causally influence reward scores.

**Phase 2: Multi-Method Causal Circuit Tracing.**

Tier A (both 7B PRMs — budget: 60 H100-hours): (a) Relevance Patching (RelP) for efficient, faithful gradient-based circuit discovery across all components simultaneously — requiring only 2 forward + 1 backward pass per sample, validated on Qwen2-7B with Pearson r=0.956 faithfulness (~15h across 2 PRMs on 1000+ contrastive samples). (b) Activation patching at every attention head and MLP layer with contrastive pairs to measure causal effect on step-level reward scores, providing cross-validation of RelP findings (~45h across 2 PRMs).

Tier B (1.5B PRM — budget: 35 H100-hours): Attribution graphs using cross-layer transcoders via CLT-Forge on Skywork-o1-Open-PRM-Qwen-2.5-1.5B, at the demonstrated-feasible scale for CLT training. This produces complete feature-level circuit maps for representative examples.

**Concrete CLT fallback:** If CLT training on the 1.5B PRM exceeds 45 H100-hours or reconstruction loss exceeds 2× the per-layer SAE baseline, we fall back to Tier A methods only (RelP + activation patching on both 7B PRMs), which constitute two independent causal methods sufficient for cross-validation.

Components are classified as fluency-encoding, reasoning-encoding, or mixed only when at least two methods converge.

**Phase 2b: Streamlined Self-Repair Quantification.** We quantify self-repair following McGrath et al. (ICML 2024) in two stages:

(a) *Attribution-based survey* (cheap: ~5 H100-hours). Use RelP-derived attribution scores to approximate self-repair ratios SR(C) = (|DE(C)| - |TE(C)|) / |DE(C)| for all identified fluency-encoding components across N≥500 test examples, where DE(C) = direct effect and TE(C) = total effect. This provides distributional estimates (median, IQR, 5th/95th percentiles) of self-repair across all components.

(b) *Focused path patching* (targeted: ~15 H100-hours). For the top-10 components with highest estimated SR from stage (a), perform exhaustive path patching with LayerNorm freezing on N≥200 examples per component. Decompose self-repair into downstream attention compensation (ΣΔ DE_h), downstream MLP compensation (ΣΔ DE_m), and LayerNorm scaling (ΔDE_LN). Compare single-site vs. multi-site ablation to test H4.

**Phase 3: Multi-Granularity Intervention Comparison.** Three CORE granularities and two EXTENSION granularities:

**Core granularities (all 3 PRMs × 3 core benchmarks):**
(i) Feature-level: SAE feature suppression on output-score-filtered bias features (our improved SteerRM-style approach with from-scratch SAEs + Arad et al. filtering);
(ii) Neuron-level: CIRM-style correlation-based neuron identification with causal mediation (median replacement), adapted to PRMs — comparing Spearman correlation selection against Xu et al.'s L1-norm probe pruning as alternative identification methods;
(iii) Circuit-level: targeted ablation/dampening of causally-validated fluency circuits while preserving reasoning circuits, using path patching for precise intervention.

**Extension granularities (single most informative PRM × 3 core benchmarks):**
(iv) Layer-level: blanket dampening of layers classified as predominantly fluency-encoding — the coarsest intervention, serving as a lower bound;
(v) Hybrid: circuit-informed feature suppression restricting feature-level interventions to causally-validated output-score-filtered features within identified fluency circuits — the finest-grained intervention, serving as an upper bound.

We benchmark core interventions on three core benchmarks: ProcessBench (core error detection), PRM-BiasBench (bias-specific evaluation), and RM-Bench Hard split (style-invariant adversarial evaluation). PRMBench and Socratic-PRMBench serve as extension benchmarks evaluated on the single most informative PRM across all five granularities, providing fine-grained diagnostic depth without expanding the core matrix.

**Phase 4: Actionability Assessment.** We evaluate each intervention against two complementary frameworks:

*Orgad et al.'s criteria* — (1) Comparative utility: does each intervention outperform simple baselines (fine-tuning on debiased data, prompt-based re-ranking, random component ablation)? (2) Mechanistic faithfulness: do interventions on identified components produce predicted changes? (3) Generalization: do findings hold across our two architecturally diverse 7B PRMs? (4) Specificity: do interventions affect only targeted bias, or cause broad side effects?

*Lee et al.'s scientific rigor criteria* — (1) Falsifiability: are our mechanistic claims testable and potentially disprovable? (2) Reproducibility: are intervention effects consistent across similar inputs? (3) Predictivity: can our circuit taxonomy predict intervention outcomes on held-out examples? We explicitly test Lee et al.'s three failure modes — non-specificity, inconsistency, and underdetermination — as diagnostic checks on our findings.

This produces a granularity-by-criterion matrix that, combined with our Domain Amenability Hypothesis and the contrast with Basu et al.'s clinical LM failures, provides the first structured empirical evidence for WHEN mechanistic interventions succeed.

**Domain Amenability Hypothesis — Testing and Contrast.** We argue PRMs satisfy all four domain amenability conditions, in stark contrast to clinical triage LMs: (1) Well-defined output semantics: PRM rewards are binary step-level judgments vs. open-ended clinical assessments; (2) Constrained output structure: scalar reward score vs. unconstrained text; (3) Verifiable ground truth: mathematically checkable reasoning vs. subjective triage correctness; (4) Testable specificity: fluency bias reduction measurable independently from reasoning accuracy on orthogonal benchmarks vs. entangled clinical dimensions. If our interventions succeed (>3% improvement on at least one benchmark), this provides positive evidence for the hypothesis; if they fail despite the favorable domain conditions, this significantly strengthens the case that mechanistic intervention is fundamentally limited.

**Revised Hypotheses.** H1 (Domain Amenability): PRM mechanistic interventions will show statistically significant improvements (>3% on at least one benchmark), providing positive evidence for our Domain Amenability Hypothesis — in contrast to Basu et al.'s clinical LM null result. H2 (Circuit Structure): Multi-method causal tracing will identify separable fluency-reasoning circuit structure in PRMs, with convergence across at least two analysis methods, corroborating CIRM's early-layer bias encoding and Xu et al.'s sparse reward subsystem findings. H3 (Granularity-Dependent Effectiveness): Among the three core intervention granularities, effectiveness will vary by evaluation context — circuit-informed approaches will outperform on adversarially-constructed bias probes (PRM-BiasBench), while feature-level may suffice for naturally-distributed errors (ProcessBench). H4 (Self-Repair): Self-repair (estimated via attribution-based SR ratio) will partially attenuate single-site interventions (median SR > 0.3), but multi-site simultaneous intervention will yield TE_multi > Σ TE_single, demonstrating that coordinated ablation disrupts self-repair pathways.
